claims.text: Adding approximately 2 at.% Y with controlled oxygen incorporation will form nanoscale Y2O3 dispersoids in a refractory high-entropy alloy matrix.
Vacuum arc melting followed by controlled oxygen exposure is a suitable route for producing the proposed Y2O3 dispersion.
The intended structural mediator is a fine, homogeneous distribution of thermally stable nanoscale Y2O3 particles embedded in the alloy matrix.
Y2O3 dispersoids will impede dislocation motion and produce dispersion strengthening.
The Y2O3 dispersoids will remain stable during prolonged exposure at 800–1200 °C.
The Y2O3 dispersoids will remain stable under irradiation.
The Y2O3 particles may limit grain coarsening.
The Y2O3 particles may limit defect migration and thereby help maintain irradiation resistance.
Relative to an otherwise comparable alloy without Y addition or engineered oxide dispersion, the intervention will improve yield strength and hardness by approximately 10–20%.
The intervention will improve high-temperature mechanical performance without compromising thermal stability.
The modified alloy will preserve the baseline alloy's thermal expansion behavior.
The modified alloy will preserve the baseline alloy's irradiation resistance.
The proposed benefits apply at approximately 800–1200 °C when irradiation doses and processing conditions do not cause substantial nanoparticle coarsening.
Excessive oxide coarsening or unintended phase formation would limit the proposed benefits.

The hypothesis will be rejected if the modified alloy shows less than approximately 10% statistically significant mechanical improvement or if the dispersoids substantially coarsen or dissolve during thermal or irradiation exposure.
